assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Oxidation (in terms of oxygen)
items.clue: A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.

items.label: Reduction (in terms of oxygen)
items.clue: A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen.

items.label: Displacement reaction
items.clue: A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound.

items.label: Redox reaction
items.clue: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together: oxygen lost by one substance is gained by another.

questions.stem: A metal reacts with another substance. What happens to the metal atoms during the reaction?

options.text: The metal atoms lose electrons and form positive ions.
The metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.
The metal atoms gain protons and become positive.
The metal atoms stay neutral and just join on.

questions.explanation: When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions by losing their outer electrons.

questions.stem: The reactivity of a metal is related to which property of its atoms?

options.text: Its tendency to grip its own electrons.
Its tendency to form positive ions.
How dense and hard the metal is.
The ability to form negative ions.

questions.explanation: The specification states that the reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions.

questions.stem: From their reactions with water and with dilute acids, which metal is placed highest in the reactivity series?

options.text: Copper, as it will not react with dilute acid.
Calcium, since it loses two electrons per atom.
Potassium, as it reacts fast with cold water.
Zinc, since its atoms have most mass.

questions.explanation: Potassium reacts most vigorously of all these metals with cold water, so it stands at the top of the order.

questions.stem: The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series. Why?

options.text: They are included because they are unusual metals.
They are placed there because every ore holds carbon.
They show that carbon extracts any metal from its ore.
They are reference points to compare metals with.

questions.explanation: Including them lets a metal be judged as above or below carbon or hydrogen, which is what predicts extraction and acid reactions.

questions.stem: A strip of magnesium is left in copper(II) sulfate solution. A pink-brown solid forms on the strip and the blue colour fades. Why?

options.text: Magnesium is more reactive, so it displaces the copper.
Copper is more reactive, so it displaces magnesium.
Both are metals, so they simply swap places.
The blue fades because the solution was diluted.

questions.explanation: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound, so magnesium takes the place of copper and copper metal is deposited.

questions.stem: Which mixture will produce a displacement reaction?

options.text: Copper added to zinc sulfate solution.
Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
Iron added to magnesium sulfate solution.
Copper added to iron(III) sulfate solution.

questions.explanation: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so zinc displaces copper from the solution.

questions.stem: Which metal reacts with cold water at room temperature to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen?

options.text: Zinc, which bubbles steadily in cold water.
Copper, used in pipes that carry water.
Sodium, which fizzes on the water surface.
Iron, because it rusts whenever it gets wet.

questions.explanation: Sodium is above magnesium in the reactivity series and reacts readily with cold water to give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. What are the products?

options.text: Magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas.
Magnesium chloride and water only.
Magnesium chloride and chlorine gas.
Magnesium chloride and hydrogen.

questions.explanation: A metal reacting with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen; with hydrochloric acid the salt is the chloride.

questions.stem: A piece of copper is left in dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Nothing happens, because copper is below hydrogen.
It fizzes steadily and gives off hydrogen.
It reacts, but too slowly for bubbles to show.
It dissolves slowly and turns the acid blue.

questions.explanation: Copper is the least reactive metal in the list and lies below hydrogen, so it does not displace hydrogen from a dilute acid.

questions.stem: Potassium reacts far more vigorously with cold water than magnesium does. What best explains this difference?

options.text: Potassium holds on to its electrons more strongly.
Potassium loses its outer electron more readily.
Potassium loses two electrons, magnesium one.
Potassium is a softer, less dense metal.

questions.explanation: Reactivity is related to the tendency to form positive ions, and potassium gives up its outer electron much more easily than magnesium.

questions.stem: Metals X and Y are added to dilute acid. X fizzes vigorously while Y fizzes only slowly. What does this show about the atoms?

options.text: Y gives up its outer electrons more easily than X.
X can form negative ions more readily than Y.
X forms positive ions more readily than Y.
X has more electrons in total than Y has.

questions.explanation: The vigour of the reaction with dilute acid reflects how readily the metal atoms give up electrons to form positive ions.

questions.stem: Four metals are added to dilute acid. P bubbles very fast, S bubbles moderately, Q bubbles slowly and R shows no change. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?

options.text: R, Q, S, P - slowest bubbling means most reactive.
R, P, S, Q - no reaction at all means most reactive.
P, S, Q only - R cannot be placed in the series.
P, S, Q, R - fastest bubbling is most reactive.

questions.explanation: Rate of reaction with the same dilute acid ranks the metals directly, and a metal showing no change is the least reactive of the set.

questions.stem: A bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid is labelled 0.500 mol/dm³. What does this label tell you about the solution inside?

options.text: Every 1 dm³ of this solution contains 0.500 g of hydrogen chloride.
Every 1 cm³ of this solution holds 0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride.
Every 1 dm³ of this solution contains 0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride.
0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride was stirred into 1 dm³ of water.

questions.explanation: A concentration in mol/dm³ states the amount of solute, in moles, present in each 1 dm³ of solution.

questions.stem: In terms of electrons, which statement is correct?

options.text: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain.
Oxidation is the gain of electrons and reduction the loss.
Oxidation is the loss of protons and reduction the gain.
Oxidation and reduction both involve losing electrons.

questions.explanation: This is the specification's definition of oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons.

questions.stem: A sealed flask contains 4.0 g of helium gas, He (Ar = 4). Which sample of methane gas, CH4 (Mr = 16), occupies the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure?

options.text: 16 g of methane gas, CH4
0.25 g of methane, CH4
4.0 g of methane, CH4
64 g of methane, CH4

questions.explanation: 4.0 g of helium is 1 mol and 16 g of CH4 is 1 mol. Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.

questions.stem: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure)?

options.text: 22.4 dm³ for each mole
24 cm³ for every mole
24 dm³ for each mole
2.4 dm³ for a mole

questions.explanation: The specification states that the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure) is 24 dm³.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). A student wants to use this equation to work out gas volumes at room temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the carbon dioxide has a gas volume here.
Every substance shown occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
The calcium oxide also occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
The calcium carbonate also occupies 24 dm³ per mole.

questions.explanation: The molar gas volume of 24 dm³ applies to gases only, and the state symbols show that carbon dioxide is the one gas in this equation.

questions.stem: A sample of carbon dioxide gas, CO2 (Mr = 44), has a mass of 8.8 g. What is the volume of this sample at room temperature and pressure?

options.text: 211.2 dm³ of carbon dioxide
4.8 dm³ of carbon dioxide gas
0.37 dm³ of carbon dioxide
120 dm³ of carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Amount = 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol, and volume = 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.
